item.title: HUL proposes raising annual pay cap for non-executive directors to ₹15 cr
item.description: Hindustan Unilever has proposed raising the annual remuneration ceiling for non-executive directors from ₹4 crore to ₹15 crore, or 1 per cent of net profit, whichever is lower ...
item.dc:creator: Sharleen Dsouza
item.content:encoded: Hindustan Unilever Ltd (HUL) has proposed increasing the annual aggregate remuneration limit for its non-executive directors to ₹15 crore or 1 per cent of the company's net profit, whichever is lower, for a five-year period starting April 1, 2026, the consumer goods major said in a stock exchange filing. The proposal, which will be placed before shareholders for approval through a postal ballot, represents an increase from the existing annual limit of ₹4 crore. The current remuneration ceiling was revised from ₹3 crore to ₹4 crore at the company's 91st annual general meeting in June 2024. According to the company's stock exchange filing, the proposed revised limit will remain in effect until March 31, 2031. The remuneration will be calculated in accordance with Section 198 of the Companies Act, 2013. Shareholders whose names appear in the company's register of members or list of beneficial owners as of November 6, 2026, will be eligible to vote on the resolution. The company’s board has appointed company secretary S N Ananthasubramanian as the scrutiniser for the postal ballot process.

item.title: Binance heist puts focus on rising cyberattacks by nation-state actors
item.description: The $6.3 billion Binance heist has renewed concerns over nation-state cyberattacks and AI-driven vulnerabilities, putting the security preparedness of crypto exchanges under scrutiny ...
item.dc:creator: Shivani Shinde
item.content:encoded: On October 29, the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance, reported a security hack. Roughly $6.3 billion was drained from the exchange platform, more than four times the previous record. In February 2025, Bybit reported a heist of $1.5 billion. The incident once again brings into focus cyberattacks led by nation-state actors, as well as the rising incidence of such attacks due to the use of AI. In India, the Binance incident perhaps brought back memories of the WazirX security incident. In July 2024, the platform suffered a major cyberattack and lost about $235 million from a multi-signature wallet managed by Liminal Custody. While cyberattacks on crypto exchanges have increased in recent times, the Binance hack has had a severe impact. First, it is the largest heist so far. Second, considering that Binance is one of the largest players and a major liquidity provider for futures trading, particularly in India, the incident assumes significance. Third, users will evaluate platforms based on the wherewithal they have to deal with such hacks. The most significant step that Binance took was the way the company accepted accountability and assured users that their investments would not be impacted. This was done immediately, which perhaps is one of the reasons there has been no panic among users. Binance was quick to say in a post on X that it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not its users. “We have already set aside more than 100% of the funds required to cover the loss. As of October 31, 2026, 98% of the impacted token assets have been replenished and are verifiable on our Proof of Reserves page. We are in the process of purchasing the outstanding, more illiquid assets,” said the company. The company, in its latest comment, said: “We have taken immediate action to contain the incident and strengthen the systems involved. The entry points identified as having been used in the attack have been closed. Systems touched in the attack path have been rebuilt or replaced. We have also implemented tighter device controls, enhanced wallet-service risk controls and expanded AI-based behavioural anomaly detection.” Binance also said that the investigation highlighted that the attack was sophisticated and a multi-stage campaign. It was not a single, isolated breach or a simple phishing incident. The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering through fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise and an advanced transaction-authorisation method. The human factor More importantly, social engineering also played its role. This once again brings into focus the role of humans in such attacks. An investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) linked the Binance hack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor. When asked why nation-state actors have been successful in hacking systems even when they have strong key management systems, Jayant Dave, CISO, APAC, Check Point Software Technologies, who has tracked at least seven major crypto thefts since 2024, said that none had broken the cryptography. His findings were that five began with a staff member’s or supplier’s device, token or session. Four involved a supplier. In four cases, people approved the malicious transaction. “State-linked groups are patient and well-funded, and they go where the defence is thinnest. Strong key management makes the vault hard to crack. So they target what is allowed to ask the vault to open: an engineer’s laptop, a supplier’s tool, an approval screen. The FBI attributes Binance to North Korea’s TraderTraitor. US and Japanese authorities have warned for years about this group’s lures aimed at engineers,” he shared in an email response to Business Standard. In its post on the modus operandi, Binance said that social engineering was also part of the hack. The attackers used a fake job interview, an internal AI tool and a stolen deployment token to reach the internal wallet signing service and start transactions outside the normal withdrawal process. Saurabh Sharma, Lead Security Researcher at the Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT) at Kaspersky, agrees with the assessment of nation-state actors' operations. He said that in such cases, attackers rarely break the keys. “They target the people and systems that are already trusted to use those keys. That is why these groups focus on engineers, developers and executives,” he said. In 2025, Kaspersky researchers detailed how BlueNoroff, a Lazarus subgroup, used fake video calls and fake recruiters to compromise people working in the crypto industry. Even experienced specialists can be caught out, as in the case of a blockchain developer who lost $500,000 after installing a fake code editor extension. “Once inside a trusted device, attackers can work through the organisation’s own approval processes. Technology alone cannot stop that if one compromised system is allowed to carry too much authority,” he added. State-linked groups are known for this kind of patience. Kaspersky’s analysis of Lazarus’s Operation FlashHole found a campaign that had been active since at least July 2025, with tools reworked over time to make it more persistent. “For investigators, it also means the first compromised device is rarely the full story. Every access point has to be traced and closed before systems can be trusted again. Exact timelines, however, can only be confirmed once the investigation is complete,” said Sharma. Lessons for Indian players From a security perspective, experts say Indian exchanges are already a target. Sharma shared that the GhostCall and GhostHire campaigns uncovered by Kaspersky have targeted Web3 and cryptocurrency organisations in India since at least April 2025. “The priority should be to make sure no single compromise can move funds. Developer and DevOps machines should be kept separate from systems that approve withdrawals, with independent checks for high-value transfers. This matters because valid accounts and trusted relationships remain leading entry points in the attacks our teams investigate,” he said. Dave says that this is not just an India-specific issue; every market faces this challenge. “Rules and audits confirm the right controls exist. The attackers behind these thefts test whether those controls hold under pressure. They are patient, and they work through people, devices and suppliers. That calls for testing alongside compliance,” he added. Dave also feels that India has built one of the more structured frameworks in the region and that it continues to strengthen it. He points to the CERT-In’s 2022 directions, which require incidents to be reported within six hours and logs to be kept for 180 days. “Crypto service providers must keep KYC and transaction records for five years. FIU-IND registration brings exchanges into the anti-money-laundering framework. Its 2026 guidelines add a cyber security audit by a CERT-In-empanelled auditor. Fast reporting and good logs are exactly what investigators need after an incident like this,” he shared. Though security experts have laid out what needs to be done, it is ultimately up to the players to take security seriously. “At CoinSwitch, we follow a risk-based approach to managing wallet exposure and withdrawals, with a focus on minimising potential vulnerabilities. This includes limiting exposure to online wallets, implementing layered access controls, transaction monitoring and withdrawal safeguards,” said Balaji Srihari, VP, Business, India, CoinSwitch. “We also emphasise segregation of duties and restricted access to critical systems to reduce insider-related risks. These controls are periodically reviewed and tested through security assessments and audits, helping us strengthen our preparedness against evolving external threats as well as potential internal risks,” he added. Nischal Shetty, founder of WazirX, said that security cannot be treated as a one-time exercise or a box to be ticked. It needs to be an ongoing priority, embedded into the way businesses operate. “Cybersecurity is not a crypto-specific challenge; it is a financial ecosystem-wide concern. Traditional banking, fintech and cryptocurrency are all exposed to an increasingly sophisticated threat landscape. However, the scrutiny on the crypto industry is understandably higher, given the direct involvement of funds and the greater difficulty of recovering stolen assets compared to traditional banking. This makes security an especially critical responsibility for the industry,” he added. Shetty also said that with the rapid advancement of AI, the industry is seeing an expanding vulnerability landscape, with new risks emerging across the software libraries, operating systems, browsers and server infrastructure that underpin modern products. “This makes it increasingly important for companies to look beyond preventive security measures and have a plan in place for worst-case scenarios,” he added.

item.title: Sebi eases digital KYC rules for NRIs, foreign nationals from December 3
item.description: Sebi will allow NRIs, OCIs and foreign nationals in FATF-compliant countries to complete KYC digitally from December 3, easing onboarding and investment in Indian markets ...
item.dc:creator: Khushboo Tiwari
item.content:encoded: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Wednesday relaxed know-your-customer (KYC) requirements for persons resident outside India (PROIs), allowing those in Financial Action Task Force (FATF)-compliant countries to complete digital onboarding without being physically present in India. The revised framework, effective December 3, will cover non-resident Indians (NRIs), overseas citizens of India (OCIs), and foreign nationals. Clients residing in FATF non-compliant countries will continue to follow existing KYC requirements. The move aims to ease onboarding and thereby investments by such investors in the Indian markets.  Under the revised norms, intermediaries can accept digital submission of KYC information and supporting documents from eligible clients. The regulator has also made KYC records portable, allowing them to be shared across intermediaries irrespective of whether all individual attributes have been validated. Intermediaries can rely on KYC undertaken by another Sebi-registered intermediary or an entity regulated by another financial sector regulator, based on records obtained from KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs) or the Central KYC Records Registry. The framework requires intermediaries to collect passport copies and, where applicable, OCI cards. Overseas addresses will be accepted as proof of address. Clients can submit KYC forms digitally or physically, while specimen signatures can be submitted electronically, subject to verification during video-based in-person verification. Sebi has mandated the presence of an authorised official during video verification and subjected the process to concurrent audit. Intermediaries will remain ultimately responsible for client KYC, including enhanced due diligence based on risk profiles. Intermediaries must provide completed KYC information to KRAs within three working days. The revised provisions will also apply to re-KYC of clients in FATF-compliant countries.

item.description: Trump made his comments in separate interviews as Americans voted in pivotal midterm elections in which the unpopular Iran war has been a key factor ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US, Iran remain far apart on deal as Trump signals no rush to strike

US, Iran remain far apart on deal as Trump signals no rush to strike Trump made his comments in separate interviews as Americans voted in pivotal midterm elections in which the unpopular Iran war has been a key factor

Fears have grown that the conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February could flare up again after midterms | WANA via REUTERS

Reuters DUBAI 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 04 2026 | 9:31 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday, as US President Donald Trump declined to rule out a resumption of US combat operations after the elections in the United States.   Trump made his comments in separate interviews as Americans voted in pivotal midterm elections in which the unpopular Iran war has been a key factor and as mediator Qatar stepped up efforts to avert a renewed escalation.   Overnight, the United States carried out "defensive" strikes on Iran's Qeshm island, targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said. Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations.

Trump on Tuesday renewed warnings of military action in an interview with the Fox News Channel. "I'm not looking to ... kill lots of people," he said. "If we have to, we'll have to."   In an interview with the Financial Times, Trump suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. Also Read

"We seem to be getting everything we want," the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.   The FT said it asked Trump about what it called "strong hints" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be an attack later this week.   "I'm ready, we're ready. We're locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it," he replied.

Trump told the FT indirect negotiations with Iran about its stockpile of enriched uranium were ongoing. "We're having discussions, and we'll see how that all works out," he said.   Also on Tuesday, Trump made a surprise announcement of a deal with Netanyahu under which Washington would stop $4 billion in annual funding to Israel after this year, but would sell weapons to its close Middle East ally. The remarks appeared aimed at swaying voters unhappy with US support for Israel.   Fears have grown that the conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February could flare up again after Tuesday's midterms.

"Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington," the senior Iranian official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks on a version of a draft US-Iran deal discussed over the past eight days.   "Tehran's conditions must be met if the US wants Hormuz reopened," the Iranian official cautioned, referring to Iranian demands including waiving oil sanctions, ending the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds.   Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, later said the US response to Iranian demands "was not convincing", adding that Washington "must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them".

"Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened," he wrote on X.  'WE CANNOT LOSE HOPE'   Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said both the United States and Iran were reviewing proposals put forward by mediators. While the Qatari team that travelled to Tehran had returned to Doha, talks were continuing.   "There are intensive joint regional efforts underway to avoid escalation," he told a news briefing, adding that Qatar remained hopeful a deal could still be reached to pave the way for future negotiations.   "If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations... and as a mediator, we cannot lose hope," he said.

An official briefed on the talks said feedback from Washington and Tehran was expected within the next 36 hours.   A senior Iranian official told Reuters later on Tuesday that there is no deadline for exchanging messages with Washington through mediators or reviewing responses.  'FORCEFUL RESPONSE'   The senior Iranian official said Tehran would not accept Washington's "excessive demands" and that nuclear talks could begin only after Iran's conditions were met.   Tehran would respond forcefully, in the region and beyond, to US strikes, the official added.   Oil prices slipped in early trade on Wednesday as investors awaited the results of the midterm elections and their potential impact on peace talks, even after industry data showed US crude stocks unexpectedly fell last week.

Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said the ball was in Washington's court after a "strong and rational response" from Tehran.   "The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit," Qalibaf said. He said Tehran's response to any US miscalculation would be unpredictable and unconstrained by geography.   The head of Iran's armed forces general staff, Ali Abdollahi, said Iran's military was updating target lists that included US and Israeli assets and would respond immediately to any threat.   Hardline newspaper Kayhan said on Tuesday that US facilities in Britain, Italy, Greece, Romania, Albania and Cyprus could be targeted in the event of renewed war.

IRANIAN-SAUDI TALKS   Alongside indirect exchanges between Tehran and Washington, regional powers are pursuing diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation. The conflict has also widened, with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis stepping up attacks on Saudi Arabia.   Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Tuesday talks with Saudi Arabia were continuing to seek new regional security arrangements that would exclude foreign military involvement.   Last week, senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian counterparts in Tehran, the first such high-level contacts since August.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
